The Great spotted kiwi (Apteryx maxima) is the largest extant member of its genus, with adults exhibiting pronounced sexual size dimorphism in body mass. Females ultimately attain a substantial adult body mass of approximately 3300 grams [Wwi = approximately 3300 grams], whereas males reach a notably smaller maximum wet weight of 2600 grams [Wwi = 2600 grams] in mature individuals. At hatching, the precocial chick emerges with a wet weight at birth averaging 325 grams [Wwb = 325 grams], a relatively large neonate compared to other ratite species. The incubation period, which proceeds under controlled thermal conditions in the mound nest, lasts 79 days [ab = 79 days] at an average temperature of 31 °C [T = 31 °C], reflecting the slow developmental pace typical of large-bodied palaeognaths.

Reproductive output in Apteryx maxima is remarkably constrained by the energetic demands of producing a single massive egg per clutch. Females lay one egg per clutch [N_R_i = one egg per clutch], and field records indicate they typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], an exceptionally low annual reproductive rate even by kiwi standards. The nestling period is brief for a bird of this size; fledging occurs only 6 days after hatching [tx = 6 days after hatching] when maintained at a stable incubation temperature of 31 °C [T = 31 °C], a consequence of the highly precocial developmental strategy that allows chicks to forage independently almost immediately. This abbreviated period of parental dependency stands in stark contrast to the protracted developmental timelines seen in many other flightless birds of comparable adult mass.

Sexual maturation in the Great spotted kiwi proceeds gradually, with puberty occurring at 100 days after hatching [tp = 100 days after hatching] under the thermoneutral conditions of 31 °C [T = 31 °C] typical of the species' burrow environment. Basal metabolic demands in this species are substantial, reflecting its large body size and endothermic physiology. Respirometry trials conducted on resting adults under standard conditions recorded a maximum basal metabolic rate of 951 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 951 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a chamber temperature of 31 °C [T = 31 °C]. This metabolic expenditure is consistent with the energetic costs of maintaining a large body mass in a cool, humid environment where thermoregulatory demands are considerable. Longevity records for the species indicate an impressive maximum lifespan in the wild of 9125 days [am = 9125 days] when individuals experience the moderate thermal conditions of 31 °C [T = 31 °C], placing Apteryx maxima among the longer-lived of the extant ratites.

The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg is 425 grams [Ww0 = 425 grams], representing one of the largest egg-to-female mass ratios among all extant birds. This enormous investment in a single offspring is a defining life-history feature of the species, and it constrains nearly every subsequent developmental parameter. Under the stable incubation conditions of 31 °C [T = 31 °C], the prenatal development period lasts 79 days [ab = 79 days], producing a highly developed chick that is already one-third of adult female mass at hatching. The combination of a massive initial egg, a relatively long incubation at 31 °C [T = 31 °C], and a rapid fledging interval of only 6 days after hatching [tx = 6 days after hatching] together illustrate a reproductive strategy geared toward producing large, precocial offspring that can immediately exploit available food resources in the challenging forest floor environment.
